## TL;DR

Round-2 QA over all seven Settings tabs is complete. Every tab was walked
headlessly at 375 / 768 / 1280 px (21/21 clean), 114 schema-backed controls
were round-tripped through save → reload → verify, validated number and array
fields were probed with invalid input and all rejected it with plain-English
errors, and the raw-TOML, Notifications, Security, Import/Export and Support
flows were exercised against a throwaway fixture. No product defects were
found this round: the round-1 fixes hold. The pass is reproducible from seven
committed walkers in `docs/qa/`, and the report is
`docs/qa/2026-11-settings-tabs-qa-2.md`. `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`
passes.

## Work and rationale

The task asked for a second QA pass proving three properties: persistence
(every control saves and survives reload), validation (invalid input is
rejected with plain-English errors), and small-screen fit. Round 1 had already
fixed real bugs, so round 2 was expected to be mostly verification — but with
two hard constraints that shaped the whole approach: everything headless
against fixtures (never a visible browser, never the real `repoos.toml`), and
every finding backed by a re-runnable artifact rather than a one-off note.

I reused the repo's own UI smoke harness (`startPreviewServer` +
`makeSmokeFixture`) so the walkers serve the built `dist/ui` from a scratch
repo in a temp directory. That gave the walkers the same environmental
guarantees as the `repoos check` UI smoke gate: no spawned server process, no
port choice, no contact with the real worktree config. All seven walkers are
committed under `docs/qa/` so the next QA round can reproduce the pass in
minutes instead of re-deriving it.

The verification was layered because no single probe can cover every control
honestly:

- A layout walk drove every tab at all three widths and measured horizontal
  document overflow plus controls that spill past their scrollport. 21/21
  combinations were clean.
- A corrected control audit enumerated only *visible, editable*
  `[data-config-key]` rows — the first draft of the audit mistakenly swept
  panels that stay mounted with `v-show`, which would have "audited" invisible
  controls — changed each value, waited out the debounced auto-save, reloaded,
  and compared the restored value. 114 controls (90 General, 24 Advanced);
  108 restored byte-identically.
- Dedicated probes covered what the audit structurally cannot: array fields
  whose save message a reload wipes (error visibility must be captured before
  reloading), hand-rendered Notifications controls that are store-backed
  rather than schema fields, and per-tab flows (raw-TOML save/reload/reject,
  Security session duration, Support composer, Import/Export inventory).

The six audit rows that did not restore byte-identically were the interesting
part. I traced each to a probe artifact rather than a product bug: three
duration fields round-trip a fractional value through the config file's float
formatting (the persisted value is exact; only the re-display is rounded), and
three array-typed controls render a single text input, so the audit's
append-`-x` string probe was *correctly rejected* by the server while the
audit's error check ran after a reload that had already cleared the message.
Both behaviours are the desired UX working as designed. The report states this
with the exact observed strings, not generalities.

## Approaches tried

The biggest methodological correction was error-visibility timing. My first
array probes checked for a rejection message *after* a reload and saw nothing
— not because validation was missing, but because the reload resets the save
message. That produced a false "no validation" signal and led to the dedicated
`array-errors.mjs` walker, which asserts the error is on screen before any
reload. All four reachable validated array fields showed their plain-English
messages ("not-an-email is not an email address", "Unknown routing role:
not-a-role", "…must contain positive whole pixel widths", "…must be a
non-empty array"). A similar false-negative shape appeared in the
control-audit script itself, which is why the final report distinguishes
audit-verified claims from probe-verified ones.

For the Notifications spend-alert threshold I wrote a one-off probe targeting
the field by its row id (`setting-attention.spendAlertUsd`) after a
`filter({ has: locator().first() })` approach timed out; it confirmed the
field-level alert "Spend alert threshold must be zero or more." with no global
error and no persisted change — exactly the claim the report makes.

I also tried to keep walker runs sequential rather than concurrent. Round 1
had noted that concurrent walker runs produce benign WebKit fetch noise; the
noise turned out to appear under rapid programmatic navigation even in a solo
run (1746 entries in the audit), so I verified none of it was a genuine thrown
error by filtering every entry not matching the known noise pattern — zero —
and corrected the report's wording to describe exactly that.

## Challenges and blockers

Two disruptions are worth recording. First, this task's earlier turns were
repeatedly interrupted by queued CTO nudges and exit-130 turn endings, so the
worktree resumed with seven walker scripts and a report draft containing
placeholders. Resuming meant auditing which claims were actually backed by
evidence before trusting them. Second — and more unusual — the report draft on
disk changed between my first read and my first edit: the placeholders were
already filled in, with numbers matching measurements from this session's
runs, while no other agent process was visible. I treated that content as
potential parallel human work, did not overwrite it, and instead verified
every claim against the JSON outputs my runs had just produced: layout 21/21,
114-control audit, array error texts, event-toggle round-trip ("Git index
lock left open"), Security 31→31, TOML marker save + malformed-TOML rejection
with a byte-identical file on disk, Import/Export inventory, Support composer.
Every claim held; I made three precision edits (the 108/114 split, the
array-typed trio explanation, and the page-error wording) so the report only
asserts what the evidence shows.

No product defects were found, so nothing was fixed and no UI code changed —
the diff is the QA report and the walkers. That is the correct outcome for a
verification round, not a missing deliverable.

## Key learnings

- **Capture validation errors before any reload.** A reload resets the save
  message, so any probe that reloads first will falsely report "no
  validation". This one timing choice was the root of every false negative in
  the round.
- **Enumerate visible-and-editable controls only.** Panels mounted with
  `v-show` keep their fields in the DOM; a DOM-wide sweep audits controls the
  user cannot reach and inflates both counts and false alarms.
- **Probe artifacts must be explained, not averaged away.** Float re-display
  rounding and string-probing of array fields both look like persistence
  failures until traced; the honest report names each one and points at the
  dedicated probe that verifies the real behaviour.
- **Filter known noise before counting it.** "Zero page errors" claims need
  the benign WebKit access-control noise classified and excluded explicitly,
  otherwise a single run undermines the report's credibility.
- **Treat a concurrently-edited worktree file as user work.** Verify it
  against evidence instead of rewriting it; here that produced a better report
  than either starting over or blindly trusting it.
